MVP CONTEXT — Echo Pages

Product Vision
Echo Pages is a minimalist, AI-assisted poetry platform where emotions get decoded into words. The site acts as a digital extension of the Instagram page—less noise, more depth. Brand vibe: introspective, raw, intelligent, slightly haunting.

Core Objective (MVP Scope)
Convert short-form Instagram poetry into a long-form, immersive reading experience using AI-generated layouts, themes, and metadata—without overengineering.

Target Users

Readers who doomscroll poetry at 2 AM

Writers who feel but can’t articulate

People who save poems but never comment
Emotionally curious, aesthetically picky, attention-poor.

Core Features (Only what moves the needle)

1. Landing Page
First impression = mood.

One powerful line (rotates daily via AI prompt)

Subtle animation, dark/light toggle

CTA: Read | Create

2. Poetry Feed

Card-based poem display

Title + poem + emotion tag (generated via AI)

Scroll = dopamine, but calm

Share-to-Instagram button (non-negotiable)

3. Poem Detail Page

Focus mode (no distractions)

AI-generated background gradient/image based on poem sentiment

Estimated “emotional weight” meter (soft metrics, not cringe)

4. Create with AI (Admin-first, public later)

Input: raw lines / keywords / emotion

AI expands, refines, or restructures poem

Choose tone: melancholic, hopeful, livid, nostalgic

Manual edit before publish (human still in charge)

5. About / Philosophy Page
Not a resume. A manifesto.
Why Echo Pages exists.
Why words echo longer than voices.

Tech Stack (AI Studio–friendly, MVP-grade)

Frontend: HTML + CSS + minimal JS (or React if you’re feeling spicy)

AI Layer: Google AI Studio (text generation + sentiment analysis)

Database: Supabase / Firebase (poems, tags, timestamps)

Auth: Admin-only login for now (keep it clean)

Hosting: Vercel / Netlify

No over-optimization. Ship first, polish later.

Non-Goals (aka stay in your lane)

No social login chaos

No comments in MVP

No recommendation engine yet

No “like” addiction mechanics

This is poetry, not a casino.

Success Metrics (Early Signals)

Avg time spent per poem

Instagram shares per post

Returning readers

Poems created per week

If people linger, you’re winning.

Brand Tone Rules

Never explain emotions

Never sound motivational

Never chase trends

Always leave a pause after reading

**Envisioning Echo Pages**

I've been solidifying the core concept: a minimalist poetry platform, Echo Pages, powered by AI. I'm imagining a landing page that showcases a single, impactful AI-generated line daily. The Poetry Feed will display poems in card format, including title, text, and an AI-assigned emotion tag. Finally, I'm brainstorming the Poem Detail Page with focus mode, AI-driven backgrounds, and an "emotional weight" metric.


**Expanding the Scope**

I'm now expanding the focus to include an "About" section and a core philosophy for Echo Pages. I'm also firming up the visual direction; I want something introspective, raw, and minimalist, with a dark/light mode toggle. Tech-wise, I'm leaning heavily towards React, Tailwind CSS, and Gemini AI. My plan is to start with a `metadata.json` file, followed by the basic structure of the app, and then the critical state management setup. I'll build a dedicated AI service (`geminiService.ts`) to handle all the AI-related tasks.


**Crafting Initial Content**

I'm focusing on the first batch of poems. For the visual identity, I've chosen a serif font for the poems and a sans-serif for the UI. Color-wise, it's a deep charcoal/black for dark mode, creamy white for light mode, and muted teal, faded crimson, or subtle violet for accents. I'm also planning slow fades and smooth scrolls. Furthermore, I've outlined the specific prompts for the AI, like using `gemini-3-flash-preview` for generating the daily line and analyzing sentiment.

️    “I did what I came here to do. I’m happy with the life I’ve lived.”

On February 1, 2019, Margaret (Marg) Anne Elizabeth Chorney was set free from her physical shell as she had finally completed her duties on this earth. 

Remaining here to share the legacy of her quick wit, bright blue eyes and unconditional love, is her husband Paul, her three children Paul (Nadine), Andrea and Christopher (Tara); and the shining lights of her world, her grandchildren, Connor and Grace. Marg will also be dearly missed by her brother, David (Cathy) in Burlington as well as her sister, Jane, in Australia. Marg also shared a truly meaningful friendship with our “Fourth Sibling”, Bobbi (Gary). 

Waiting with open arms to welcome Marg home are her beloved parents, Arthur and Beatrice and younger brother, Peter, as well as several extended family members and friends. 

Family was everything to Marg and she took great pride in raising her children in a house full of love. She created many beautiful memories filled with warm meals, laughter, summer getaways to Muskoka and Prince Edward Island, camping adventures, many dogs over the years, and cozy winter nights around a warm wood stove. 

Mom faced multiple sclerosis (MS) and later breast cancer with an indomitable strength and optimism. She embodied the philosophy that while we can’t choose what life throws at us, we do choose how we deal with it. She did so with much laughter and love. 

Heartfelt thanks go to her caregivers over the years from ParaMed and the staff at Hillsdale Terrace (Pine Ridge) who became second family to her. 

Friends and family are invited to a Celebration of Life on February 24th, 2019 from 1 p.m. to 4 p.m. at Mountlawn Funeral Home, 21 Garrard Rd, Whitby, Ontario. Refreshments will be provided. Tributes begin at 1:30 p.m. 

In lieu of flowers, donations can be made to Multiple Sclerosis Society of Canada, Breast Cancer Society of Canada, the Heart and Stroke Foundation or a charity close to your heart. 

Marg’s light, warmth and resilient spirit will shine in our hearts forever.

1. Auth & User Profiles (Non-Negotiable)

Echo Pages moves from anonymous vibes to ownership & credibility.

Every poem upload is tied to:

Authenticated user (email / OAuth / magic link)

Persistent User Profile

Public credit: “Echoed by @username”

User profile shows:

Total poems uploaded

Genre-wise contributions

Weekly performance stats

Cumulative score (visible only to the user for now)

This sets the foundation for creator economy mechanics later. No auth = no long-term product.

2. Leaderboard System (Weekly Cadence)

Add a Weekly Leaderboard that resets every Sunday.

Logic:

Poems are tagged with a detected genre using LLM classification.

Each poem gets a genre match percentage (0–100).

Higher accuracy = higher score.

Leaderboard rules:

Top users of the week based on average poem score

Visible publicly (username + rank only)

Detailed breakdown visible inside user account

This creates:

Friendly competition

Habit formation

Return traffic every Sunday

Basically: retention engine unlocked.

3. Genre Match Percentage (Accuracy Upgrade)

Current genre detection works, but MVP needs more signal, less noise.

Improvement approach:

Combine:

LLM semantic classification

Keyword overlap scoring

Genre confidence weighting

Final score = weighted average, not single-shot LLM output.

This reduces false positives and makes scores feel earned, not random.

4. Profanity & Censored Content Filter

Zero tolerance for garbage input.

Before any poem is stored:

Run Regex-based profanity scan (fast, cheap)

If borderline → pass through LLM moderation check

If flagged:

Block submission

Show soft warning to user (no shaming, just UX)

Result:

Platform stays clean

LLM costs optimized

No toxic content leakage

5. Rate Limiting (Abuse Control)

Implement request throttling per user + IP.

Rules:

Max X poem submissions per minute

Max Y API calls per IP per hour

Temporary cooldown if exceeded

This prevents spam, scraping, and accidental overload.

6. Edge Case: DDoS / Suspicious Activity

If multiple high-frequency requests from same IP:

Trigger caution state

Log event

Temporarily restrict actions (not full ban)

This is not military-grade security—
but for MVP, this is responsible engineering.

**Building the MVP Framework**

I'm currently focused on the core architecture needed for "Echo Pages." I've been researching the most sensible approach to the user authentication system, with a preference for either email/magic link or OAuth login options for the initial MVP. I'm keen on using Supabase for its simplicity. My immediate priority is integrating user accounts and then tying each poem to a user profile, displaying basic stats, such as total poems and genre contributions, that can be added to the profiles.


**Enhancing the Platform Features**

I've been occupied with the integration of new features. Specifically, I'm working on the weekly leaderboard, which will rank users by the average poem score, reset every Sunday. This score will be based on improved genre match accuracy.  I'm also implementing a more robust moderation system using a fast Regex approach with an LLM fallback. I've updated the `types.ts` file to include these new data points and created the necessary components to display user profiles and leaderboards. Finally, I'm incorporating request throttling to improve the overall performance.


**Incorporating New System Logic**

I'm now integrating new system logic. I've decided to leverage Supabase's built-in Auth, simplifying the process. I'm focusing on modifying `echoes` and `admin_poems` tables to include `user_id`, and I'll create a `profiles` table logic through Supabase. I'm also updating `geminiService.analyzePoem` to return a "genre match score". For the frontend, I'm working on a minimalist, dark, high-contrast, typography-focused design. This includes the new components: `Auth.tsx`, `Profile.tsx`, and `Leaderboard.tsx`.


**Adding Detailed System Features**

I'm currently working to integrate and refine key aspects. I've decided to incorporate a genre-specific scoring system, allowing the LLM to analyze how well a poem aligns with a selected genre. I'm building weekly leaderboard logic through timestamp filtering, implementing a robust profanity filter with regex and LLM fallback. The `Profile` component will feature usernames, stats, and a personalized feed. I'll need to update `types.ts`, `geminiService.ts`, and `supabaseService.ts`, as well as several components, including `Profile.tsx`, `Leaderboard.tsx`, and `Auth.tsx`. Due to limitations, I will implement a username/email login for the MVP demonstration.


**Initiating Authentication Logic**

I'm now starting on the authentication logic, leaning towards Supabase Auth UI patterns to keep things streamlined. My goal is to incorporate a username/email login for the MVP. I'm focusing on the integration of user authentication and account management within the Supabase framework.

The vision for **Echo Pages Phase-2** transforms the platform from an anonymous stream into a competitive, high-integrity sanctuary for poets. 

### Specification

**1. Authentication & Ownership**
- **Auth System:** Integrated Supabase Auth (Email/Magic Link). A new `Auth.tsx` component handles entry.
- **Profiles:** Users have persistent profiles showing their cumulative score and genre mastery.
- **Credit:** Every echo is now attributed to a `@username`.

**2. The Scoring Engine (Genre Match)**
- When creating a poem, the user selects a target **Genre** (e.g., Noir, Haiku).
- **Gemini Service** analyzes the text and provides a **Confidence Score (0-100)** based on how well the poem adheres to the linguistic traits of that genre.
- This score determines the user's rank on the leaderboard.

**3. Weekly Leaderboard**
- A new view accessible from the header.
- Displays top contributors based on **Average Accuracy** for the current week (resets Sundays).
- Features a minimalist "high-score" aesthetic consistent with the dark theme.

**4. Hardened Safety (Profanity Filter)**
- Multi-layer check: 
    1. Local regex for common slurs (instant).
    2. Gemini-based moderation for context-aware toxicity.
- Rejected content is never stored; the user is gently notified.

**5. Visual Identity**
- Scores are displayed as thin "Confidence Bars" next to poem titles.
- Profile pages use the same "spectral noise" and haunting gradients to maintain the digital sanctuary vibe.

To fix the **400 Error** with Google Auth, the most common culprit is a mismatch between the URL your app sends and what Supabase has in its "Allowed" list.

### 1. The Code Update
I've made the `redirectTo` logic more robust to ensure it matches exactly what Supabase expects (handling trailing slashes) and added clearer error handling in the UI.

### 2. The Dashboard Configuration (Required)
The code alone cannot fix a 400 error if the Supabase Dashboard isn't set up. You **must** do the following in your [Supabase Dashboard](https://supabase.com/dashboard):
1.  **Authentication > URL Configuration**: 
    *   **Site URL**: Set this to your production URL (e.g., `https://echo-pages.vercel.app/`).
    *   **Redirect URLs**: Add your production URL again but with a wildcard: `https://echo-pages.vercel.app/**`.
2.  **Authentication > Providers**:
    *   Ensure **Google** is enabled.
    *   Ensure you have entered a **Client ID** and **Client Secret** from the [Google Cloud Console](https://console.cloud.google.com/).
    *   Ensure you have added the **Authorized Redirect URI** provided by Supabase into your Google Cloud project's OAuth settings.

New user registration is not working properly.

Improve spacing, alignment, and contrast.

Group information cleanly.

This is an MVP — keep solutions simple and stable.

Do not over-engineer.

Do not redesign the entire UI.

Do not introduce unnecessary new features.

Bug-fixed authentication and navigation

Clean, maintainable code changes

Clear comments where logic changes

Treat this as a real product MVP, not a demo.

Based on your description of the signup failure—specifically the empty `{}` error—here is a diagnostic checklist of the most likely causes for failure at the MVP stage.

### 1. Supabase Dashboard Configuration (The Most Likely Culprit)
*   **Email Confirmation Setting:** By default, Supabase requires users to confirm their email before they are considered "active." If a new user signs up but the app tries to log them in immediately, it will fail.
    *   *Check:* Go to **Authentication > Providers > Email**. Is "Confirm email" toggled **ON**? For an MVP, toggling this **OFF** allows instant access.
*   **Email Provider Enabled:** Ensure that the "Email" provider is actually toggled **ON** in the same section.
*   **Site URL & Redirects:** Supabase needs to know where to send users after signup/login.
    *   *Check:* Go to **Authentication > URL Configuration**. Ensure the "Site URL" matches your current deployment or development environment (e.g., `localhost:5173`).

### 2. Database Triggers & Public Schema (The "Silent" Killer)
*   **Profile Sync Triggers:** It is common to have a PostgreSQL trigger that automatically creates a row in a `public.profiles` table when a new user joins `auth.users`.

*   **RLS (Row Level Security) Policies:** If your signup logic relies on inserting data into a public table immediately, ensure the RLS policies allow "service_role" or "authenticated" (or anon for signup) to perform those inserts.

*   **Mismatched Keys:** Ensure the `SUPABASE_URL` and `SUPABASE_ANON_KEY` in your environment exactly match the ones provided in your Supabase project settings.

2.  **Check Supabase Logs** (Authentication > Logs) to see the exact error message the server is sending.

Based on the behavior you described—especially the **`{}`** error display and the delayed failure—here is a diagnostic checklist to identify why your Supabase Auth signup is failing.

### 1. The "Confirm Email" Requirement (Most Common)
By default, Supabase projects have **Email Confirmation** enabled. When a user signs up, Supabase creates the user record but marks them as "unconfirmed." 
*   **The Symptom:** The signup call succeeds at the API level, but if your code immediately attempts to log the user in or perform a database action (like creating a profile), it fails because the user session isn't "active" yet.
*   **Check:** In Supabase Dashboard, go to **Authentication > Providers > Email**. Toggle **Confirm email** to **OFF** for testing.

### 2. Database Triggers & Constraints
Many Supabase setups use a PostgreSQL trigger to automatically create a row in a `public.profiles` table whenever a new user is added to `auth.users`. 
*   **The Symptom:** If your database schema has a constraint (e.g., a `username` column is marked `NOT NULL` but your trigger doesn't receive that data), the database transaction will fail. This causes the entire `signUp` request to fail and roll back.
*   **Check:** Go to **Database > Error Logs** or **Authentication > Logs** in the Supabase Dashboard. Look for "Postgres Error" or "Foreign Key Constraint" errors.

### 3. Rate Limiting (The "Developer" Trap)
Supabase has a strict default rate limit on how many signups can originate from a single IP address to prevent bot spam.
*   **The Symptom:** If you have been testing signup repeatedly, you may have hit the "Signup Rate Limit."
*   **Check:** Go to **Authentication > Settings > Rate Limits**. Check the "Max Signups per Hour" setting. Also, check the **Authentication > Logs** to see if "Too Many Requests" (429 error) is being logged.

### 4. Password and Email Constraints
*   **Password Length:** Supabase has a default minimum password length (usually 6 characters). If your UI doesn't enforce this but the backend does, it will reject the attempt.
*   **Disposable Emails:** There is a setting to block disposable email providers. If you are using a "test" email service, it might be blocked.
*   **Check:** Verify the password length in **Authentication > Settings > Password Strength**.

### 5. Why the error shows as `{}`
The reason you see `{}` instead of a message is a common JavaScript UI quirk. 
*   **Explanation:** The Supabase SDK returns an `AuthError` object. If the code tries to render that object directly (e.g., `setError(error)`), JavaScript's default stringification for Error objects often results in an empty object `{}`. 
*   **Meaning:** An error **is** being caught; the UI is just failing to "unpack" the text description of it.

### 6. Provider Conflicts (Google vs. Email)
If you previously signed up with Google using the same email address you are now trying to use for an Email/Password signup:
*   **The Symptom:** Supabase may block the creation of a second "identity" for the same email address depending on your "Link identities" settings.
*   **Check:** Go to **Authentication > Settings**. Look for **"Allow unverified email identities"** or settings regarding account linking.

1.  **Check Supabase Auth Logs:** This is the absolute truth. Go to **Authentication > Logs**. Every failed signup attempt will have an entry there with a specific status code and error message (e.g., `422`, `429`, or `500`).

You will **not** find the Gemini API Key value anywhere in your folder structure or source code. This is a security feature to ensure your key is never accidentally leaked to the public (e.g., when you push your code to GitHub).

To get your exact API Key value to paste into Vercel, follow these steps:

### 1. Get your key from Google
1.  Go to the **[Google AI Studio](https://aistudio.google.com/app/apikey)**.
2.  Sign in with your Google account.
3.  Click on the **"Get API key"** button on the left sidebar.
4.  Click **"Create API key"** (either in a new project or an existing one).
5.  **Copy the long string of characters** that appears. That is your `API_KEY`.

### 2. Paste it into Vercel
1.  Open your project dashboard in **Vercel**.
2.  Navigate to **Settings** > **Environment Variables**.
3.  In the **"Key"** field, type: `API_KEY`
4.  In the **"Value"** field, paste the string you copied from Google AI Studio.
5.  Click **Add**.
6.  **Redeploy** your project for the changes to take effect.

### Why this is better:
*   **Security**: If you push your code to GitHub, anyone can see your files. If the key were in a file, anyone could steal your credits/quota.
*   **Best Practice**: Using `process.env.API_KEY` is the standard "Senior Engineer" way to handle secrets in modern web development.

payload.text:
When a user publishes a poem without providing a title, the system should auto-generate a title using Gemini LLM, so poems aren’t published as “Untitled”.
When it triggers
✅ On “Publish”
Only if title == null OR title.trim() == ""
Input
Poem text (required)
Optional metadata:
author pen name
language
mood tags (if any)
Output
generated_title (string)
title_source: "USER" or "AI"
Optional: title_confidence (0–1)
UX
If title missing:
Show generated title pre-filled
User can edit/override before publishing
Button: “Regenerate” (max 2–3 times to prevent abuse)
Acceptance Criteria (MVP)
If no title → a title is always generated
Title length target: 2–8 words
No offensive content
Avoid generic trash like “A Poem” / “My Thoughts” unless poem is too short
MVP Feature 2: Automatic Genre Detection (from fixed list)
Goal
Detect the poem’s genre from your fixed genre set:
"Noir", "Ethereal", "Minimalist", "Free Verse", "Prose", "Haiku", "Lyric", "Narrative", "Elegy", "Ode", "Sonnet", "Ballad", "Spiritual", "Mystical", "Philosophical", "Existential", "Fragmentary", "Gothic", "Dark Poetry", "Macabre", "Psychological", "Confessional", "Personal", "Meta-Poetry", "Ars Poetica", "Surreal", "Absurdist"
When it triggers
On publish OR after draft save (your call)
MVP best: trigger on publish only (cost control)
Input
Poem text only (required)
Output
predicted_genre (one string from list)
genre_score in percentage (0–100)
Optional: top_genres list
Example output:
{
"predicted_genre": "Ethereal",
"genre_score": 86,
"top_genres": [
{"genre": "Ethereal", "score": 86},
{"genre": "Mystical", "score": 73},
{"genre": "Lyric", "score": 62}
]
}
Acceptance Criteria (MVP)
Always returns exactly 1 genre
Returns a confidence %
Doesn’t hallucinate new genres
Works even on short poems (fallback behavior defined)
MVP Feature 3: “Genre Match %” + Color Bar UI
Goal
Show the user how closely the poem matches the predicted genre using:
a % score
a horizontal progress bar
bar color based on score (stronger = “more green / more intense”)
UI Spec
Component
Label: Genre: Ethereal
Subtext: Match: 86%
Bar: filled to 86%
Color mapping suggestion
0–39% → Red (weak match)
40–69% → Yellow/Orange (medium)
70–100% → Green (strong match)
Acceptance Criteria
% appears as an integer
Bar color changes correctly based on thresholds
Bar fill corresponds to percentage

To help you ace your assignment submission, here is a breakdown of how to answer potential questions from your faculty. These talking points are categorized by design philosophy, technical architecture, and the specific AI implementation.

### 1. The Design Philosophy: "Why Echo Pages?"
*   **Minimalism & Introspection:** Explain that the UI is intentionally sparse to focus the user’s attention on the poetry. The use of "Instrument Serif" and "Playfair Display" creates a "digital sanctuary" vibe.
*   **The Anti-Social Network:** Unlike Instagram or X, there are no "likes" or "comments." The only metric is **Resonance** (how well the AI thinks the poem fits its genre). This removes social pressure.
*   **Atmospheric Experience:** Mention the "spectral noise" overlay and the dynamic gradients generated by the AI to match the poem’s mood.

### 2. Technical Stack & Architecture
*   **Frontend:** Built with **React** for state management and **Tailwind CSS** for the high-end aesthetic.
*   **Backend-as-a-Service (BaaS):** You used **Supabase** for real-time data persistence, user authentication (OAuth), and separate data streams for "Curated" (Admin) vs. "Community" (Echoes) content.
*   **Real-time Sync:** Explain that the app uses Supabase's PostgreSQL Realtime to update the feed instantly when a new "Echo" is published across all users.

### 3. AI Implementation (The "Brain")
*   **Gemini 3 Integration:** You used the `gemini-3-flash-preview` model via the `@google/genai` SDK.
*   **Literary Analysis:** The AI acts as a "literary critic." It doesn't just store text; it analyzes the content to predict a genre, suggest a title (if missing), and calculate a "Resonance Score."
*   **Structured Output:** Mention that you used **JSON Response Schemas** to ensure the AI returns data in a strict format that the app can parse without errors.
*   **Safety & Moderation:** The AI performs a "spectral analysis" on every poem before publication to ensure it meets community safety standards, acting as an automated moderator.

### 4. Special Features: The Watermark & IP Protection
*   **Protection against Screenshots:** If asked about the dense watermark, explain that it's a "Visible Watermark" strategy. It deters unintended reuse and ensures that even if a poem is screenshotted, the **Echo Pages** brand identity is preserved.
*   **SVG Pattern Tiling:** Technically, this is implemented using an inline SVG as a `background-image` that repeats. It is low-opacity so it doesn't obstruct readability but high-frequency so it's impossible to crop out.

### 5. Potential "Tough" Questions & Answers
*   **Q: "Why did you use AI for the titles instead of letting users write them?"**
    *   *A: "Users can write titles, but the AI provides a fallback 'Suggested Title' to maintain the atmospheric quality of the feed if the user feels uninspired."*
*   **Q: "How do you handle the API Key security?"**
    *   *A: "The API key is handled through environment variables (`process.env.API_KEY`), ensuring it is never hard-coded in the source files."*
*   **Q: "Why is the Resonance score important?"**
    *   *A: "It gamifies the writing process in an introspective way. It rewards 'Mastery' of a specific genre, which is reflected in the Leaderboard rankings."*

### Final Tip:
When presenting, refer to the app as a **"Full-stack AI-Integrated Literary Platform."** It shows you understand not just how to build a UI, but how to integrate complex AI logic and cloud databases into a cohesive product. Good luck with your assignment!

payload.text:
1. Post Management: Edit & Delete (User-Owned Content)

Non-negotiable feature. If users can create, they must control.

Edit Post

Only the author can edit their poem.

Editing updates the content but preserves:

original creation timestamp

engagement metrics (likes, saves, etc.)

Optional but classy: show a subtle “edited” badge.

Delete Post

Only the author can delete.

Hard delete vs soft delete:

MVP-friendly: hard delete (remove row).

Scalable version: soft delete (is_deleted = true) for analytics and recovery.

Deleting a post should:

Remove it from all feeds (home, profile, followers’ feeds).

Cascade delete or detach likes/comments (no orphan data).

This is basic data hygiene. Anything else is amateur hour.

2. Follow System (Instagram-style, but quieter)

We’re introducing a social graph without turning Echo Pages into a noise factory.

Core Concepts

Any user can follow any other user.

Each user has:

Followers count

Following count

Followers list

Following list

Think adjacency list, not magic.

Follow / Unfollow

Toggle-based action.

Idempotent: clicking follow twice doesn’t duplicate rows.

Instant UI feedback (optimistic update).

Data Model (conceptual)

Users table

Follows table:

follower_id

following_id

created_at

No counters stored blindly. Either compute or carefully cache.

3. Feed Prioritization (This Is the Secret Sauce)

This is where Echo Pages differentiates.

Behavior

When a user follows someone:

Any new poem posted by that author appears at the top of the follower’s feed.

Feed ordering logic:

Posts from followed users (most recent first)

Then global / discovery poems

Not algorithmic chaos. Just intentional signal > noise.

Why this matters

Rewards intentional following.

Encourages meaningful connections.

Prevents the feed from becoming a random poetry landfill.

Later phases can add ranking. For now: deterministic > “AI vibes.”

4. Word Limit Removal (Creative Freedom Mode)

This is a philosophical decision, not just a technical one.

What changes

Remove minimum (10) and maximum (200) word constraints entirely.

Poems can be:

one-liners

prose-poems

long spirals of thought

What stays

Optional UI hint: “Write freely.”

Backend safety:

character cap at database level (for abuse prevention, not creativity policing).

This aligns with Echo Pages’ core identity: expression without rails.

👎 Dislike

dislike or

do nothing

Toggle Logic

Like → Dislike = switch state

Like → Like again = remove reaction

Dislike → Dislike again = remove reaction

This is standard reaction-state management. Anything else is buggy behavior dressed as UX.

This is the important part. Very Echo Pages.

Per-user preference

Each user can choose:

Show like/dislike counts

Hide counts entirely

Just like Instagram’s “hide likes,” but extended to dislikes too.

Important nuance

Reactions still exist even if counts are hidden.

Backend always stores real counts.

UI just respects user preference.

This avoids:

Performative posting

Popularity contests

Engagement anxiety

Creators write. Readers react. Numbers don’t scream unless invited.

Reactions table

user_id

poem_id

reaction_type (like | dislike)

created_at

Uniqueness constraint:

(user_id, poem_id) must be unique

This prevents duplicate reactions and keeps logic sane.

Counts can be:

calculated on demand (safe for MVP)

cached later if scale demands it

No premature optimization nonsense.

8. Feed Behavior with Reactions

Let’s be explicit so future-you doesn’t hate past-you.

Likes/dislikes do NOT reorder feeds (yet).

Feed priority is still:

Followed users’ latest poems

Others

Reactions are feedback, not ranking fuel.
Echo Pages ≠ TikTok casino.

Later, if you want:

soft discovery boosts

mood-based surfacing
That’s Phase 5 territory.

The data model updates in `types.ts` include `likesCount`, `dislikesCount`, and a `userReaction` field. I am adding user profile fields for followers, following counts, and a preference to hide reactions. The state management in `App.tsx` handles followed IDs and user preferences.

I've set length restrictions at 1 and 10000 characters. Finally, I'm using `auth.updateUser` to implement user-controlled reaction visibility.
